original_question: Can every infinite achievable set be decomposed as the algebraic sum of two achievable sets of Hausdorff dimension 0?
target_in_paper: Section 3, Problem 16, posed immediately after Theorem 13 in the section "Algebraic sums and decompositions of achievement sets."
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper's actual problem. It correctly captures the universal quantifier (every infinite achievable set), the decomposition into a sum of two achievable sets, and the intended strengthening from measure-zero summands to summands of Hausdorff dimension 0.
missing_details: The ambient space is the real line: the problem concerns one-dimensional achievable subsets of R.
An "achievable set" means a set that arises as the achievement set of some absolutely convergent real series, i.e. a set of subsums of the form {sum ε_n x_n : ε_n in {0,1}}.
The sum should be stated explicitly as the algebraic/Minkowski sum A+B = {a+b : a in A, b in B}.
The Hausdorff-dimension-0 condition applies to each of the two summand sets individually.
The problem is restricted to infinite achievable sets; finite achievable sets are excluded.
Problem 16 itself does not impose extra structural assumptions such as 'Cantor', 'central Cantor', 'homogeneous', or 'multigeometric' on the two summands.

The nearby context matters: Theorem 13 already proves decomposition into two achievable Cantor sets of Lebesgue measure zero, and Problem 16 asks whether this can be sharpened to summands of Hausdorff dimension 0.
refined_question: Let E subseteq R be an infinite achievable set, meaning that E is the set of subsums of some absolutely convergent real series, E = {sum_{n=1}^infty ε_n x_n : ε_n in {0,1}}. Must there exist achievable sets A,B subseteq R such that dim_H(A)=dim_H(B)=0 and E=A+B:= {a+b : a in A, b in B}?
justification: The paper states in Section 3 that every infinite achievable set is already known to be the algebraic sum of two achievable Cantor sets of Lebesgue measure zero (Theorem 13). Immediately afterward, it asks the sharper open problem whether every infinite achievable set can be written as the sum of two achievable sets of Hausdorff dimension 0 (Problem 16). Your draft matches this official formulation almost verbatim, but it leaves implicit the ambient space R, the precise meaning of 'achievable set' as a set of subsums of an absolutely convergent real series, and the exact meaning of the sum operation. The nearby context also shows that no extra restrictions on the summands are part of Problem 16 itself; the later discussion of homogeneous Cantor sets and semi-fast convergent sequences belongs to a related question, not to Problem 16.
